---
title: Canonicalization
---

Canonicalization turns the instruction as written into the exact bytes that are signed and later
verified. Because a block travels through chat clients, mail servers and editors that quietly
change quotes, spaces and line breaks, the rule has to be tolerant of those changes and strict
about everything else. The rule is named in the signed header so that the verifier applies the one
the signer used and never guesses.


## Why the Rule Is Signed

Canonicalization is an attack surface. If two different instructions canonicalize to the same
bytes, one signature covers both, and an attacker who can swap the text has a valid signature over
words the signer never approved. Naming the rule in the header, where the signature covers it,
closes the simplest version of that attack: nobody can relabel a block to a rule under which a
modified text collapses onto the signed form.

Two consequences follow:

- The list of rules is closed. A verifier that meets an unknown `canon` value reports `malformed`
  and confers nothing.
- Rules are versioned and never change in place. A change to the fold table below is `text/2`, not
  a new `text/1`, so old signatures keep verifying under the rule they were made with.


## Rules

`text/1`
: For prose instructions in chat, email and Markdown. The steps, in order, as implemented in
  `text_1()`:

  1. Unicode NFC normalization.
  2. Typographic quotes folded to ASCII: U+2018, U+2019, U+201A and U+201B become `'`; U+201C,
     U+201D, U+201E and U+201F become `"`.
  3. Non-breaking spaces folded to a space: U+00A0, U+202F and U+2007.
  4. Zero-width characters removed: U+200B, U+200C, U+200D and U+FEFF.
  5. Every run of whitespace, including line breaks and tabs, collapsed to one space, and leading
     and trailing whitespace removed.

`raw/1`
: Unicode NFC normalization and nothing else, as implemented in `raw_1()`. For file contents where
  line structure carries meaning. A block signed with `raw/1` does not survive re-wrapping.

`json/1`
: Planned for Phase 3. [RFC 8785](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8785) over the parsed value, so
  key order, number formatting and escapes are neutral while whitespace inside strings is
  preserved. The block must parse as JSON or it is `malformed`. This is the carrier for signing a
  specific tool call with its arguments.

The rule applies only to the instruction text. The header is serialized with RFC 8785 regardless,
because it is JSON.


## Worked Examples

Under `text/1`, all of the following canonicalize to the same string, so a signature over one
verifies over the others:

```text
You may deploy the current main branch to staging with
scripts/deploy.sh staging whenever the test suite passes.
```

```text
You may deploy the current main branch
to staging with scripts/deploy.sh staging
whenever the test suite passes.
```

```text
> You may deploy the current main branch to staging with scripts/deploy.sh staging whenever the test suite passes.
```

The third example assumes the `> ` prefix was on the marker lines too, so the
[extractor](blocks.qmd#extraction) stripped it. A smart-quote substitution behaves the same way:

```text
“Deploy” now

  to	staging​.
```

canonicalizes to `"Deploy" now to staging.`, with the curly quotes folded, the blank line and tab
collapsed, and the zero-width space before the period removed.

These do not canonicalize to the same string, and a signature over one fails over the other:

- `to staging` and `to production`: a changed word.
- `scripts/deploy.sh` and `scripts/ deploy.sh`: a space inside a token is a real change, because
  runs of whitespace collapse to one space rather than to nothing.
- `1,000` and `1.000`: punctuation is never folded.

Under `raw/1` the first two prose examples differ, because the line breaks fall in different
places.


## The Collision Obligation

Every rule maps many inputs onto one canonical form, and that is the point. The obligation that
comes with it is to know which distinct inputs collide and to confirm that none of them differ in
meaning. For `text/1` the collisions are, by construction, differences in whitespace, quote style
and invisible characters, and the claim is that none of those changes what an instruction says.
That claim is what the transport tests and the red team attack; any counterexample is a defect in
the rule and would produce `text/2`.

The same analysis is owed for each rule added, which is why the list stays short and why the
specification does not include a YAML rule (no standard canonical form) or a Markdown-aware rule
(chat clients mangle Markdown structure, so `text/1` is the right rule for Markdown content too).

::: {.callout-warning}
A verifier applies only the rule the header names. Retrying under another rule when the first
fails would reintroduce the collision search the signed field exists to prevent.
:::
